raw_case_text:
A 35-year-old man admitted to our emergency center (Imam Ali Hospital, Kermanshah, western Iran in 2017) with complaint of palpitation, dyspnea and nonproductive cough for recent three weeks. His past medical history except for temporary paroxysmal palpitation was unremarkable. Chest x-ray revealed a dumping in the lower right cardiac border (Fig. 1). Routine laboratory exam including, complete blood count, BUN, creatinine and, NA, K were unremarkable but hepatic function tests were abnormally high. Sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein were in abnormal high ranges. Arterial blood saturation in room air was normal. The routine coagulation profile was normal. Cardiac enzymes were in the normal range.
The patient was not feverish, the pulse was 112 beats/min, and the respiration rate was 22/min. The blood pressure was 110/65 mm Hg. He was tachypneic and tachycardic and had low blood pressure (80/50 mm gH). The physical exam also showed the signs of right atrial tamponade with rapid, weak pulse with paradoxical nature, jugular veins were distended and accentuated with inspiration. The physical exam showed, moderate hepatomegaly (3 cm below of costal ridge), pitting lower extremities edema, and vague heart sounds. The lungs sound was clear, and the neurologic examination was unremarkable. Electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm at a rate of 118 beats/min with normal intervals with no ST segments change in the cardiac leads. The electrocardiogram showed low volt QRS height, with T-wave flattening in all of the ECG leads. Due to lung air interposition, a transthoracic echocardiogram was unremarkable without obtaining a diagnostic benefit, and a transesophageal two-dimensional echocardiogram was denied by the patient.
The cystic lesion closely attached to the surrounding cardiac structures, most probably representing a hydatid cyst (Fig. 1). CT scan was added to imaging modality that showed a large para cardiac cystic mass closely related to cardiac structures (Fig. 2).
With the impression of ruptured hydatid cyst, the patient scheduled for open surgery performed by midline sternotomy and with beating off-pump approach. During intraoperative inspection, he had an intrapericardial cystic mass compressing the right atrium and inferior border of the right hemi-diaphragm. There was mild sero-sanguineous pericardial effusion (Fig. 3). The cystic mass had a thick wall with severe inflammatory reactions. Its cavity contained necrotic, fibrinous, and thrombotic materials with some pasty like materials without the presence of the daughter cyst or typical germinal layer as seen in the HC (Fig. 4). The medial wall of cystic mass was attached densely to the right atrium and compressed its cavity. The cyst cavity was filled by thrombotic material caused by presence of small (3 mm) defect in the medial wall of cyst. The venous blood from right atrium leaked to cyst cavity. For prevention of cardiac injury, medial wall of cyst left open to pericardial cavity, but others part as lateral borders adhered to partial pericardium was easily released and excised.
Erosion of cyst wall to thin atrial wall caused silent bleeding to cyst cavity and subsequent thrombus formation. No connecting vascular pedicle from cyst to aorta or great vessels was found. On histopathological exam, some evidence of necrotic, fibrinous and thrombotic material with an inflamed pericardial layer were found and no malignant tissue or cells were detected (Fig. 5).
The postoperative course was uneventful and discharged in 6 th day of operation and in the 6 th months of follow-up, no recurrence of effusion was detected by TEE as his clinical condition was good.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old Iranian man presented with a 3-week history of palpitations, dyspnea, and nonproductive cough.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the emergency department with progressive palpitations, shortness of breath, and dry cough over the preceding 3 weeks.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of transient paroxysmal palpitations; otherwise unremarkable past medical history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for palpitations, dyspnea, and dry cough; negative for fever.

objective.physical_examination: Afebrile, tachycardic (pulse 112-118 bpm, weak and paradoxical), tachypneic (22 breaths/min), and hypotensive (blood pressure dropping from 110/65 to 80/50 mmHg) with clinical signs of right atrial cardiac tamponade: distended jugular veins with inspiratory accentuation (Kussmaul's sign), muffled heart sounds, moderate hepatomegaly (3 cm below the costal margin), and bilateral pitting lower-extremity edema. Lung fields were clear.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC, BUN, creatinine, electrolytes, coagulation profile, cardiac enzymes, and room-air arterial oxygen saturation were normal, while liver function tests, ESR, and CRP were elevated. ECG showed sinus tachycardia (118 bpm) with low-voltage QRS complexes and diffuse T-wave flattening. Chest X-ray showed a prominent bulge along the lower right cardiac border. Transthoracic echocardiography was non-diagnostic due to pulmonary air interposition.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic CT revealed a large paracardiac cystic mass closely attached to and compressing the right atrium. Off-pump median sternotomy identified a thick-walled, severely inflamed intrapericardial cystic mass compressing the right atrium and right hemidiaphragm with mild serosanguineous pericardial effusion; the cyst contained necrotic, fibrinous, pasty, and thrombotic material (secondary to a 3-mm erosion defect communicating with the thin right atrial wall) with no daughter cysts or germinal membrane. Histopathology confirmed an inflamed pericardial cyst containing necrotic, fibrinous, and thrombotic debris without parasites or malignancy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Inflamed and thrombosed intrapericardial cyst with a 3-mm right atrial wall erosion causing right atrial tamponade (initially suspected to be a ruptured cardiac hydatid cyst, which was excluded by the absence of daughter cysts or germinal layer intraoperatively and on histopathology). Following median sternotomy, lateral cyst wall excision, and decompression into the pericardial cavity, the patient was discharged on postoperative day 6 and had no recurrence on 6-month follow-up TEE.
